outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of *Santos v. Kimmel*, detailing the factual scenario involving former Congressman George Santos and host Jimmy Kimmel. It outlines the mechanics of the 'Cameo' platform deception, the subsequent airing of the videos on *Jimmy Kimmel Live!* ('JKL'), and the specific causes of action filed by Santos. The chapter concludes by explaining the District Court's dismissal under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) and defining the standard of appellate review applied by the Second Circuit.
subtopics: The Cameo Deception: Facts regarding fictitious name submissions and video creation
The 'Will Santos Say It?' Segments: Contextualizing the broadcast usage
District Court Dismissal: Grounds based on fair use and preemption/failure to state a claim
Standard of Review: De novo analysis under Rule 12(b)(6) and judicial notice

outline.chapter_title: Copyright Infringement and the Fair Use Doctrine
outline.description: This section provides a deep dive into the court's primary legal analysis regarding federal copyright law. It breaks down the four statutory factors of fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107 as applied to these specific facts. Special emphasis is placed on the 'transformative' nature of the secondary use, addressing Santos's argument about his subjective intent versus a reasonable observer's perception. The chapter also clarifies why bad faith allegations (regarding Kimmel's lies) do not negate fair use and analyzes why no market harm occurred despite the public mockery.
subtopics: Statutory Framework: The four factors of fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107
Purpose and Character: Transformative use vs. subjective intent (citing *Warhol* and *Goldsmith*)
Good Faith Defense: Why misrepresentation did not invalidate fair use (addressing *Harper & Row*)
Nature of Work and Amount Used: Published status and scope of copying
Market Effect Analysis: Distinguishing market substitution from devaluation via parody/criticism

outline.chapter_title: Analysis of State Law Claims: Contract Preemption and Pleading Standards
outline.description: Here, the text examines why Santos's state law claims failed, focusing first on why preemption arguments were rendered moot by independent pleading failures. It details the court's application of Illinois law regarding third-party beneficiaries to reject the direct breach of contract claim against Cameo's Terms of Service. Furthermore, it explains New York law requirements for implied-in-fact contracts, highlighting the insufficiency of conclusory allegations regarding a 'meeting of minds.' This chapter serves as a primer on how federal copyright policy interacts with state contract theories in digital platform disputes.
subtopics: Preemption Overview: Why resolving preemption was unnecessary due to pleading defects
Direct Breach Claim (Illinois Law): Third-party beneficiary presumption in Terms of Service agreements
Implied Contract Claim (New York Law): Failure to allege essential terms and meeting of minds
